Consult Summary:
- 27-year-old man with 3 days of profuse, watery diarrhoea (hourly while awake), crampy central/lower abdominal pain, nausea with one vomiting episode after milk, subjective fever and reduced urine output—most consistent with acute infectious gastroenteritis; oral rehydration and symptomatic care recommended with safety-netting if not improving in 48 hours.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Profuse watery diarrhoea for ~3 days, occurring approximately every hour while awake; stools described as very loose/“just pouring.”
  - Intermittent crampy abdominal pain, central/lower abdomen; pain severity ~6/10 when present.
  - Nausea and at least one episode of vomiting after consuming milk.
  - Subjective feeling of being hot (no measured temperature).
  - Decreased urinary frequency compared with baseline.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began ~3 days ago (Monday/Tuesday → present on day 3).
  - Not improving; patient reports persistent high stool frequency.
  - Brother has had a similar illness for ~5 days and is improving.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Patient reports symptom provocation after milk (vomiting); drinks fluids but feels they “go straight through.”
  - Avoiding alcohol and heavy foods while symptomatic; advised clear fluids and soft diet.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - Nausea, vomiting (after milk), subjective fever/feeling hot.
  - No reported blood in stool.
  - No other systemic complaints documented.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No measured fever documented.
  - No blood in stool per patient recall.
  - No history of chronic GI disease reported.

Past Medical History:
- Reports otherwise “fit and well”; no chronic medical conditions recalled.
- Family history: father currently with stage 3 colon cancer (patient not fully certain of details).

Medications:
- Current / recent:
  - Paracetamol taken as needed (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - No regular medications.
- Allergies:
  - No known drug allergies (per patient).

Social History:
- Lives with mother and sister; brother does not live with him.
- Occupation: works in an office in Central London (government).
- Tobacco: social smoker (occasional, e.g., on Fridays).
- Alcohol: occasional heavy episodic drinking 1–2 times/month.
- No other substance use documented.
- Financial or lifestyle factors: prefers to continue working where possible; hesitant to take time off.

Family History:
- Father with stage 3 colon cancer.
- Brother recently had similar diarrhoeal illness (~5 days).

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Exam findings: Not recorded (telehealth visit; no physical exam documented).

Investigations:
- No laboratory tests or imaging performed or available.
- No stool studies ordered or results available.
- Clinician advised symptomatic management; no objective vitals obtained.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Acute infectious gastroenteritis—most likely viral etiology (e.g., norovirus), given acute onset, profuse watery diarrhoea, crampy pain, nausea/vomiting, subjective fever, and a household/close-contact with similar illness.
- DDx Integration (brief):
  1. Acute viral gastroenteritis — High likelihood.
     - Supporting: 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea, crampy abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, subjective fever, brother with similar illness.
     - Opposing: No measured fever or objective exam/vitals.
  2. Bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis — Medium likelihood.
     - Supporting: Profuse diarrhoea, cramping, subjective fever; possible shared exposure with brother.
     - Opposing: No bloody stools reported; course and household clustering favor viral.
  3. Secondary (post-infectious) lactose intolerance — Medium likelihood.
     - Supporting: Vomiting after milk; transient lactase deficiency can follow enteric infections.
     - Opposing: Broader hourly diarrhoea and household case favor transmissible infection.
  - No conflicts between the transcript and the DDx summary were identified.
- Issue 1: Acute diarrhoea / presumed viral gastroenteritis
  - Assessment:
    - Acute, likely self-limited gastroenteritis (probable viral cause), 3 days duration with high stool frequency and crampy pain.
  - Plan:
    - Rehydrate: oral rehydration solution recommended (Dioralyte — OTC) and frequent clear fluids.
    - Diet: clear fluids initially; progress to soft/bland diet (e.g., soup, mashed foods) as tolerated.
    - Symptomatic meds: paracetamol acceptable for fever/pain (dose/route/frequency not documented in record).
    - Antidiarrheals not discussed; no antidiarrheal recommendation documented.
    - Safety-netting: return or call back if symptoms not improving within 48 hours, or sooner for any of:
      - Signs of worsening dehydration (markedly reduced urine output, dizziness, lightheadedness, syncope),
      - High or persistent fever,
      - Severe or worsening abdominal pain,
      - Blood in stool,
      - Inability to tolerate fluids or persistent vomiting.
    - If dehydration or clinical deterioration suspected, arrange urgent assessment and possible investigations/IV fluids.
    - Follow-up: patient instructed to call clinician/clinic if not settling in 48 hours.
- Issue 2: Possible secondary lactose intolerance (transient)
  - Assessment:
    - Vomiting after milk suggests milk may exacerbate symptoms; may reflect transient lactase deficiency following infection.
  - Plan:
    - Advise temporary avoidance of milk/dairy while symptomatic.
    - Reintroduce lactose-containing foods gradually once diarrhoea resolves.
    - If persistent symptoms after resolution of acute illness, consider further evaluation for lactose intolerance (not ordered now).
- Issue 3: Dehydration risk from high stool output
  - Assessment:
    - Patient reports reduced urine frequency and subjective feeling of being hot; at risk for dehydration given hourly watery stools.
  - Plan:
    - Emphasize oral rehydration solution (Dioralyte OTC) and frequent sips of fluid.
    - Monitor urine output and general well-being; seek urgent care if signs of moderate–severe dehydration (confusion, fainting, very low urine output, rapid heart rate — note vitals not recorded).
    - Consider clinic/ED review for IV fluids and labs if dehydration suspected or if unable to tolerate oral fluids.
- General plan items:
  - Avoid alcohol until recovered.
  - Continue paracetamol PRN for fever/pain.
  - No antibiotics or further tests currently indicated unless clinical deterioration or >48 hours without improvement; stool testing or blood tests may be considered if prolonged or severe symptoms (not ordered now).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vitals (temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate) are not recorded.
  - Physical abdominal examination not recorded (telehealth).
  - No laboratory studies or stool tests documented.
  - Medication dosing/frequency for paracetamol not recorded.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None identified; DDx supports the clinician impression of likely gastroenteritis.
- Transcript quality:
  - Telehealth audio with intermittent connection issues; overall history obtainable though no physical exam possible.
